## Claim qualification

Unproven claims use these linguistic patterns:

"Trusted by the world's most ambitious AI teams" - Positioning via passive voice; shifts burden to reader to verify via logos
"Proven across every industry" - Uses past participle without evidence; appears in section heading as axiom
"World-class [attribute]" - Superlative without measurable basis (world-class RLHF, world-class annotations)
"Industry-leading [attribute]" - Superlative with industry scope undefined (industry-leading annotation)
"Best-in-class [attribute]" - Superlative used across multiple pages (best-in-class annotations, best-in-class AI software)
"Reliable AI has no shortcuts" - Maxim presented as discovered truth, not marketing claim
"The data powering the world's best AI" - Definite article construction; presupposes superiority

Pattern: Scale consistently uses adjectives (trusted, proven, best-in-class, world-class, reliable) without comparative data, measurements, or independent verification. Claims settle on logo display and industry names (Meta, Mayo Clinic, DoD) as proof substitutes.

## Conversion path

Every page follows this conversion funnel:

Entry point (hero section) -> Value propositions (mid-page features/claims) -> Social proof (logos, testimonials) -> Single primary CTA

Primary CTAs across all pages:
- "Book a Demo" or "Book demo" (appears 3-4 times per page minimum)
- Secondary CTAs: "Build AI", "Explore Data Engine", "Learn More", "Read customer story"

Conversion design: No direct signup, trial, or self-serve option visible. All conversion paths terminate at sales-assisted demo booking. No pricing page exists. No freemium model offered.

The reader receives: Value positioning + social proof + logo display. What Scale asks for: Calendar availability for a demo. No lead magnet or content download required before demo booking.

## Distinctive

Vertical-specific Data Engine pages. Rather than one generic product page, Scale maintains separate but structurally identical pages for Physical AI, Generative AI, Automotive, and Public Sector. Each uses the same template (hero, value props, three core capabilities, case study, resources) but swaps terminology, use cases, and customer logos. This is not a product differentiation; it is an organizational/sales convention. It signals: "We are data company that has learned to speak each vertical's language separately."

## Noise

Mayo Clinic partnership banner appears on at least 4+ pages (homepage, Data Engine, GenAI, others) consistently. This becomes visual clutter across the site rather than emphasis. The banner is announced as news, but its persistence as a persistent top-of-page element suggests it serves as a trust marker rather than a time-bound announcement. For a company of one, this repeating banner would be noise; for enterprise infrastructure sales, it is a normalized trust ritual.

Excessive customer logo carousels. Every page includes a customer carousel (Meta, Cohere, Adept, NTT, CDAO, Mayo Clinic, etc.). No specific use case attribution to logos. This is a convention borrowed from enterprise SaaS playbooks; without attribution, logos function as generic "we have big customers" signals rather than proof of feature fit.
